newsitem.title: USA: Lay-offs from 1996 mergers plunge; workers valued more.
newsitem.headline: Lay-offs from 1996 mergers plunge; workers valued more.

text.p: Newly merged American companies cut 46 percent fewer employees from their combined workforces in 1996 than in 1995, despite a record volume of mergers, according to an international employement agency Monday.

Mergers accounted for 42,603 job cuts, or 8.9 percent of the 477,147 jobs eliminated in 1996, as companies valued their experienced employees more highly than before, said Challenger, Gray & Christmas. This compared with 72,083, or 16.4 percent of the 1995 job-cut total of 439,882.
A record $658.8 billion worth of mergers were announced in 1996, exceeding expectations, said Challenger Gray, which tracks job-cut announcements daily.

"While corporate cost cutting is the genesis of many mergers, combined companies are re-examining their forming stance about the disposability of people, and in many cases are choosing to find positions for as many experienced employees as possible," said John Challenger, executive vice president of the Chicago-based firm.

"In the past such heavy merger activity would have signalled massive job cuts. Today we are seeing a much different picture. Companies are recognising that wholesale job slashing can ultimately hurt the bottom line by destroying corporate memory and lowering the morale of the remaining workforce."

Challenger said it was crucial for merged companies to maintain a high standard of customer service to improve their reputation and competitive edge. He said that could only be achieved when the workforce is experienced and is committed to the newly merged company.
